title: How To Produce Massive Academic Improvement In Your Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that a shift in education toward what he calls indoctrination — teachers openly promoting personal political views rather than teaching students how to think — has left a gap that any teacher willing to focus purely on academic skill can exploit to dramatically outpace their peers. His prescription is to eschew advocacy entirely and focus every lesson on strengthening core academic skills: reading, writing, and math, taught through original sources, Socratic questioning, and rigorous practice. He argues this approach builds genuinely independent thinkers capable of forming their own conclusions, rather than students who parrot borrowed opinions and collapse under light questioning. He acknowledges that curricula themselves often carry embedded viewpoints, and calls on teachers to be personally rigorous and self-aware enough to set aside their own political views while at work, regardless of what they privately believe, so that classroom time is devoted entirely to building students' capacity to think for themselves.
points: A shift toward political advocacy in classrooms, Linsin argues, has left students behind academically and created an opportunity for teachers who focus purely on skill-building.
The recommended focus is exclusively on core academic skills — reading, writing, and math — taught through original sources and rigorous practice.
Socratic questioning and exposure to primary sources and historical thinkers across the political spectrum are presented as tools for building independent thought.
Teachers are urged to set aside personal political views while teaching, even if the curriculum itself carries embedded viewpoints.
The goal is producing students who can research, argue, and even switch positions in debate, rather than repeat borrowed slogans.
quotes: You see, education has become indoctrination. It’s become teaching students what to think rather than how to think.

The result is a generation of students—66 percent of whom can’t read at grade level—spouting shallow platitudes based on omitted truths, simplistic ideas, misguided emotions, and zero depth of understanding of history and the people who lived it.
Eschew the advocacy and focus exclusively on academic skill. Yes, that means reading, writing, and math.
Rely on original sources and the great thinkers and philosophers of history from all stripes, creeds, backgrounds, and viewpoints.
If debate strengthens understanding, then let your students do the research and create the arguments themselves. And then have them switch positions.

You can be a staunch liberal or conservative in your personal life. Capitalist or socialist. But if you can set aside your views the moment you enter the parking lot , and be of good courage, you won’t believe what you and your students can accomplish.
